body.heading: One bite is a complete practice
paragraphs: Most meals are eaten the way most walks are walked: on autopilot, with the mind somewhere else entirely — in the phone, the news, the afternoon’s meeting. The food disappears and barely registers, which is a pity twice over: less pleasure, and a body that hardly noticed it ate.

You do not need to eat a whole meal in reverent silence. Start with one bite — the first bite of anything — eaten with your full attention. It takes twenty seconds and it changes the meal more than you would expect.

body.heading: How to taste one bite properly
paragraphs: Look at the food first, the way you would if you had never seen it. Notice colour and shape. Then smell it. Then take the bite and slow down: texture first, then temperature, then the flavours arriving in sequence, then the ones that linger. Chew more than habit suggests.
That is all. The rest of the meal can be perfectly ordinary — conversation, crumbs, second helpings. One attended bite is the rep; the rest is just lunch.

body.heading: Why people keep doing it
paragraphs: The attended bite has a way of spreading. People find the second bite gets a little attention too, and the meal slows by a minute or two without any effort of will. Food starts tasting like more, because more of you is present for it.
It is also the most portable mindfulness practice there is. No cushion, no app, no special time — just the next bite of the next thing you eat, wherever you already are.

takeaway: One bite, full attention: the smallest possible meditation, served three times a day.
